To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the overall impact of tax, welfare and public service pay policies on household incomes from 2009 up to 2014 is that: The highest income group lost about 151/4 per cent, mainly due to increases in taxes on income and capital gains, and reductions in public sector pay The middle income group lost about a third of this, or around 5 per cent.
the impact of the Budget 2014 is that those with the lowest household incomes lose 2 per cent, those in the middle lose 11/4 to 1 per cent, and the highest lose 13/4 percent.
the Budget 2014 was progressive in the distribution of income, while the Budgets from 2009 up to and including 2013 were regressive.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the distributional impact of Budget 2009 and subsequent Budgets up to and including Budget 2014 can be assessed.
the impact on households of the series of budget measures introduced from 2008 to 2014.
the distribution of the burden of tax, welfare and public service pay policies in Budget 2014.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the impact of Budgets since October 2008 on the distribution of household incomes has been regressive.
the impact of Budgets 2008-2013 has been regressive, but not by much.
the impact of Budgets 2008 to 2014 has been regressive, but that it has been regressive in a somewhat more moderate sense than might have been expected.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the impact of the Budgets since 2009 on household income was regressive, with those on lower incomes suffering the greatest loss, and those on higher incomes losing less.

Budget 2013 had its greatest impact on low income groups (a reduction of 2 percent), the lowest impact was on middle income groups (losses of between 11 and11/4 per percent), while the top income groups lost somewhat more (about 13/4 percent).
Budget 2013 was a very significant blow to low income groups, but that over the full period since 2009, the impact has been much more even across the income scale.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the impact of tax, welfare and public service pay policies on household incomes is very unevenly distributed, with the lowest income groups experiencing the greatest losses in real income, and the highest income group losing the least.
the impact of tax increases, welfare reductions and public sector pay reductions has been broadly similar for different income groups.
Budget 2013 was a turning point in the distribution of income impacts of tax, social welfare, and public service pay policies.
